title: August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (75/75 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Who was the original English translator for Of Grammatology?
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak translated Jacques Derrida's seminal 1967 French text De la grammatologie into English as Of Grammatology in 1976, accompanying it with an influential eighty-page scholarly preface that introduced deconstruction to the English-speaking world.

items.title: Q2 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which figure explains the meaning of the play Everyman at its conclusion?
items.explanation: In the fifteenth-century English morality play Everyman, after Everyman descends into the grave and the Angel welcomes his soul into heaven, the Doctor delivers the final epilogue summarizing the moral lesson that only Good Deeds accompany man to judgment.

items.title: Q3 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Who in his preface to Joseph Conrad’s The Secret Agent makes the following remark? “the achievement of modern art is that it has ceased to recognize the categories of tragic and comic or the dramatic classifications ‘tragedy’ and ‘comedy’, and views of life as tragicomedy.”
items.explanation: In his 1926 preface to the German edition of Joseph Conrad's The Secret Agent (1907), German author Thomas Mann remarked that modern art abandons rigid categories of tragedy and comedy, viewing human existence essentially as tragicomedy.

items.title: Q4 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: The Restoration period’s most characteristic drama, the “comedy of manners”, was gradually replaced by “sentimental drama” in response to shifts in the audience’s taste. Which of the following statements best represents the difference between these two types of comedy?
options: Comedies of manners expose human follies to laughter, sentimental comedies provoke sympathetic tears for the characters’ faults.
Comedies of manners were commercially successful; sentimental comedies were not.
Comedies of manners were critically successful; sentimental comedies were not.
Comedies of manners were written in rhymed couplets; sentimental comedies were written in blank verse.
items.explanation: Restoration comedy of manners relies on witty repartee and satirical ridicule to expose the affectations and moral vices of high society, whereas eighteenth-century sentimental comedy appeals to moral benevolence and tender pathos, evoking sympathetic tears for characters who repent.

items.title: Q5 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The epitaph on her tombstone that Emily Dickinson composed herself reads
items.explanation: Emily Dickinson's gravestone in Amherst, Massachusetts, bears the epitaph "Called Back", drawn from the title of Hugh Conway's 1883 novella and forming the entire text of the final letter she wrote to her cousins before her death in May 1886.

items.title: Q6 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Shel is a character in Virginia Woolf’s novel ……………
items.explanation: Marmaduke Bonthrop Shelmerdine, known affectionately as Shel, is the romantic seaman whom the protagonist meets on the moors and marries in Virginia Woolf's novel Orlando (1928).

items.title: Q7 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Thomas Mann described the theme of one of his fictional works as “the fascination of death, the triumph of disorder in a life founded on order.” Which of his works was he referring to?
items.explanation: Thomas Mann described the core theme of his 1912 novella Death in Venice (Der Tod in Venedig) as the fascination with death and the collapse of disciplined bourgeois order into uncontrolled passion and cholera in Venice.

items.title: Q8 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: In the middle of the story the narrator in Oroonoko digresses from the central tale of Oroonoko’s revolt and tells of various expeditions taken in company with Oroonoko. What is the purpose of these digressions, according to the narrator?
options: To illustrate the richness of the country of Surinam
To enliven the dullness of the central narrative
To give proof of Oroonoko’s daring and curiosity
To convince the reader that the narrator is indeed an eye-witness to the events described
items.explanation: In Aphra Behn's novella Oroonoko (1688), the female narrator explains that she recounts expeditions such as hunting tigers and visiting indigenous native towns expressly to give proof of Oroonoko's daring, physical bravery, and intellectual curiosity.

items.title: Q9 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In 1941 John Day Company in New York published Jawaharlal Nehru’s autobiography under the title
items.explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru's autobiography, written while imprisoned in Dehradun between 1934 and 1935, was published in Britain as An Autobiography (1936) and released in the United States in 1941 by the John Day Company under the title Toward Freedom.

items.title: Q10 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: “In honoured poverty thy voice did weave / songs consecrate to truth and liberty, – / Deserting these, thou leavest me to grieve” are lines from “To Wordsworth”. Who is the poet?
items.explanation: These lines are from Percy Bysshe Shelley's sonnet "To Wordsworth" (published in 1816), in which Shelley laments William Wordsworth's political abandonment of republican and revolutionary ideals in favor of political conservatism.

items.title: Q11 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Speaking of Siva is an English translation by A.K. Ramanujan of some …………. Bhakti poems composed by Virasaiva saints.
items.explanation: A.K. Ramanujan's Speaking of Siva (1973) is a classic English translation of devotional vacanas (free-verse lyrics) composed in Kannada by four medieval Virasaiva Bhakti saints: Basavanna, Allama Prabhu, Mahadeviyakka, and Devara Dasimayya.

items.title: Q12 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In Beowulf, Beowulf accuses Unferth of I. pagan beliefs II. killing his own “kith and kin” III. “unchecked atrocity” IV. unprovoked war The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In the Old English epic Beowulf, Beowulf responds to Unferth's drunken boast by accusing him of fratricide—killing his own brothers ("kith and kin", statement II)—and noting that Grendel's monstrous atrocities would never have raged unchecked in Heorot had Unferth possessed true courage (statement III).

items.title: Q13 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Charles Dickens opined that “no man ever before had the art of making himself mentally so like a woman since the world began.” He was acknowledging the quality of the work of which writer?
items.explanation: In an 1858 letter praising Scenes of Clerical Life, Charles Dickens astutely discerned that the pseudonymous author "George Eliot" (Mary Ann Evans) was a woman because of the exquisite psychological delicacy and understanding with which female characters were drawn.

items.title: Q14 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In his well-known essay “Politics and the English Language”, George Orwell provides representative examples of what common faults?
options: Staleness of imagery and lack of precision
Lack of precision and incorrect formatting
Incorrect formatting and staleness of imagery
Staleness of precision and lack of imagery
items.explanation: In his 1946 essay "Politics and the English Language", George Orwell identifies staleness of imagery and lack of precision as the two pervasive faults that corrupt modern political prose into vague, dishonest clichés.

items.title: Q15 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: According to Roland Barthes, the “writerly text” is
options: a unique expression of the writer’s individual genius
consumed by way of a seemingly unitary meaning
linked to active participation of the reader in the establishment of the text’s meaning
items.explanation: In S/Z (1970), Roland Barthes defines the "writerly" (scriptible) text as an open, plural work that requires the active participation of the reader as a producer of meaning, contrasted with the "readerly" (lisible) text where the reader remains a passive consumer.

items.title: Q16 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The Canadian Nobel Laureate Alice Munro is known for her
items.explanation: Canadian author Alice Munro was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2013 as the "master of the contemporary short story," celebrated for collections like Runaway (2004) and The Moons of Jupiter (1982).

items.title: Q17 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: A critical question Eliot’s Prufrock poses, so important to an understanding of his character, is
items.explanation: In T.S. Eliot's "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" (1915), the timid speaker repeatedly obsesses over his existential hesitation with the pivotal question "Do I dare?", asking "Do I dare / Disturb the universe?" and "Do I dare to eat a peach?"

items.title: Q18 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: A test of listening comprehension is a test of
items.explanation: In English language teaching methodology, listening and reading are classified as receptive skills because they involve comprehending and interpreting incoming language, whereas speaking and writing are productive skills.

items.title: Q19 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Colin Clout, Spenser’s persona in The Shepheardes Calendar appears in two of these eclogues. I. ‘June’ II. ‘February’ III. ‘November’ IV. ‘December’ The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In Edmund Spenser's pastoral suite The Shepheardes Calender (1579), Spenser's poetic persona Colin Clout speaks directly in the 'June' (I) and 'December' (IV) eclogues (as well as 'January'). Statements II ('February') and III ('November') do not feature Colin Clout as an interlocutor.

items.title: Q20 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which character in Crime and Punishment speaks of St. Petersburg as a city of half crazy people filled with gloomy, harsh and strange influences?
items.explanation: In Part 6, Chapter 3 of Fyodor Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment (1866), Arkady Ivanovich Svidrigailov remarks to Raskolnikov that St. Petersburg is a city of half-crazy people subject to gloomy, harsh, and strange influences that distort human thought.

items.title: Q21 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: At the conclusion of Swift’s Modest Proposal, the narrator declares that he has “not the least personal interest in endeavouring to promote this necessary work, having no other motive than the public good of my country.” What evidence does the narrator give that his advice is free from other motives? I. The narrator is Irish and a sworn bachelor, unlikely to father children. II. He has no children who will be affected by the scheme, and thus cannot make money from it. III. His wife is past childbearing, and thus the narrator cannot benefit by “breeding” her. IV. The narrator is English, and therefore this scheme will not affect him personally. The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In the final paragraph of Jonathan Swift's satire A Modest Proposal (1729), the narrator claims pure public-spirited motives by noting that his youngest child is nine years old (so he cannot sell infants, statement II) and his wife is past childbearing age (statement III). Statements I and IV are false because the narrator does not claim to be a bachelor or an Englishman.

items.title: Q22 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: The Grammar Translation Method was historically used in teaching
items.explanation: The Grammar Translation Method was historically developed in European schools during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries for teaching classical literature in Greek and Latin through explicit grammatical rules and direct bilingual translation.

items.title: Q23 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Most of the titles of Aldous Huxley’s novels are taken from various literary works. Match the titles of his novels with the works from which they have been borrowed : I. Brave New World A. Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell II. The Doors of Perception B. Marlowe’s Edward II III. Antic Hay C. Wordsworth’s “The Tables Turned” IV. Those Barren Leaves D. Shakespeare’s The Tempest The right code according to the key is :
items.explanation: Aldous Huxley derived his novel titles from literature: Brave New World (1932) quotes Miranda in Shakespeare's The Tempest [I-D]; The Doors of Perception (1954) borrows from William Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell [II-A]; Antic Hay (1923) quotes Christopher Marlowe's Edward II [III-B]; and Those Barren Leaves (1925) quotes William Wordsworth's "The Tables Turned" [IV-C].

items.title: Q24 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: “There is no set and there are no wings; the stage is empty and in almost total darkness. This is in order that right from the beginning the audience shall receive the impression of being present not at a performance of a carefully rehearsed play, but at a performance of a play that suddenly happens.” Which of the following plays have the above stage directions?
options: Luigi Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author
items.explanation: Luigi Pirandello's metatheatrical masterpiece Six Characters in Search of an Author (1921) begins on an empty, dark stage without scenery or wings, creating the illusion that the audience is watching an ordinary acting company rehearsal suddenly disrupted by fictional characters.

items.title: Q25 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In Thomas Hobbes’s grand metaphor in Leviathan, a commonwealth is like ………….
options: a great ship piloted by one man, but managed by the efforts of many.
an artificial man imbued with the strength of many men.
an octopus whose many tentacles represent the competing interests of men.
an ostrich, which thrusts its head in the sand to avoid danger and self examination.
items.explanation: In the Introduction to Leviathan (1651), Thomas Hobbes introduces his famous governing metaphor of the commonwealth as an "Artificiall Man", a great Leviathan of superior stature and strength created through art, wherein sovereignty is an artificial soul.

items.title: Q26 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The word “Calamus”, a kind of water reed referenced in the title Calamus Poems, is a symbol for Whitman of
items.explanation: In the "Calamus" poems added to Leaves of Grass (1860), Walt Whitman uses the sweet flag or calamus reed growing in secluded ponds as a central symbol for deep comradeship, romantic male friendship, and democratic fraternal bonds.

items.title: Q27 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Assertion (A) : The world is becoming increasingly multilingual. Reason (R) : To monolingual Anglophones it may look like everyone in the world is learning English. In the context of these two statements
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both statements are sociolinguistically true: global population growth and mobility expand multilingualism across the globe (A), and native English speakers frequently assume that worldwide learning of English equals universal adoption of English alone (R). However, (R) merely describes a monolingual Anglophone bias rather than providing the causal reason for global multilingual growth (A).

items.title: Q28 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: The first scene in Girish Karnad’s Tughlaq opens in front of a …………..
items.explanation: Scene 1 of Girish Karnad's historical drama Tughlaq (1964) opens outside the royal court of justice in Delhi, where citizens gather to discuss Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq's administration and witness the outcome of a Brahmin's lawsuit against the crown.

items.title: Q29 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: What is the final word in Joyce’s Ulysses?
items.explanation: James Joyce's modernist masterpiece Ulysses (1922) concludes Episode 18 ("Penelope") with Molly Bloom's iconic stream-of-consciousness affirmation: "...and yes I said yes I will Yes."

items.title: Q30 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which Victorian novel has the subtitle “New Foes with an Old Face”?
items.explanation: Charles Kingsley's 1853 historical novel set in fifth-century Roman Alexandria is titled Hypatia: or, New Foes with an Old Face, using historical religious fanaticism to critique nineteenth-century Tractarianism and theological intolerance.

items.title: Q31 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: In which of the following poems does W.H. Auden call 1930s “a low dishonest decade”?
items.explanation: In the opening stanza of "September 1, 1939", written in a New York dive bar at the outbreak of World War II, W.H. Auden looks back over the interwar years, describing them as "a low dishonest decade."

items.title: Q32 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Two examples of closet drama are I. Byron’s Manfred II. Shelley’s Cenci III. Marlowe’s Edward II IV. Shaw’s Widower’s Houses The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Lord Byron's Manfred (1817, statement I) and Percy Bysshe Shelley's The Cenci (1819, statement II) are celebrated examples of Romantic closet drama, composed in verse primarily for private reading rather than practical theatrical staging. Marlowe's Edward II and Shaw's Widowers' Houses were written for public stage performance.

items.title: Q33 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Who among the following postcolonial critics worked on the fiction of Joseph Conrad in his/her early career?
items.explanation: Palestinian-American critic Edward Said launched his scholarly career with his doctoral dissertation on Joseph Conrad, which was published in 1966 as his first book, Joseph Conrad and the Fiction of Autobiography.

items.title: Q34 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In The Trial what is the main character Joseph K’s job?
options: He works in a government office
items.explanation: In Franz Kafka's novel The Trial (1925), the protagonist Josef K. works as a senior officer and chief cashier in a large commercial bank at the time of his inexplicable arrest.

items.title: Q35 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following best summarises the structural approach to literature?
options: Meaning is inherent in the word itself.
A language’s history explains how it works.
Meaning is generated through relationships in a system of signs.
Binary oppositions are to be avoided at all costs.
items.explanation: Structuralism in literary studies, developed from Ferdinand de Saussure's linguistics, asserts that meaning does not exist independently within isolated words or objects, but is produced through differential relationships and codes within a larger system of signs.

items.title: Q36 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: The Australian poet A.D. Hope is best known for his I. elegies II. Satires III. Sonnets IV. Doggerel verses The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Australian poet A.D. Hope (1907–2000) established his literary reputation through his rigorous formal verse, most famously his classical satires (such as The Dunciad Minimus, statement II) and reflective elegies (statement I).

items.title: Q37 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: At the conclusion of Gulliver’s Travels, Gulliver argues that his motivation for telling the tale is
options: to assist the British nation in enlarging her colonies
to produce a travelogue of genius and learning
items.explanation: In the concluding chapter of Part IV of Gulliver's Travels (1726), Lemuel Gulliver asserts that his primary motive for publishing his travels is solely "to INFORM and INSTRUCT Mankind", disavowing any interest in literary praise or commercial entertainment.

items.title: Q38 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Match the character with the play : Character I. Everyman in His Humour II. Volpone III. Epicoene IV. The Alchemist Play A. Bonario B. Subtle C. Knowles D. Morose
items.explanation: The characters match Ben Jonson's comedies as follows: Knowell (Knowles) is the suspicious father in Everyman in His Humour (1598) [I-C]; Bonario is the honorable young heir in Volpone (1606) [II-A]; Morose is the misanthropic bachelor who hates noise in Epicoene (1609) [III-D]; and Subtle is the titular fraudulent charlatan in The Alchemist (1610) [IV-B].

items.title: Q39 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following novels by Nuruddin Farah deals with foreign aid?
items.explanation: Somali novelist Nuruddin Farah's novel Gifts (1992), the second volume of his Blood in the Sun trilogy, critically examines the destructive dependency and political compromise wrought by international foreign food aid to Somalia.

items.title: Q40 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In the house of Holinesse in Faerie Queene, Redcross learns repentance and the way to heaven from Dame Caelia and her daughters, who are named :
items.explanation: In Book I, Canto X of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590), the Redcrosse Knight receives spiritual healing in the House of Holiness from Dame Caelia and her three daughters, who personify the theological virtues: Fidelia (Faith), Speranza (Hope), and Charissa (Charity).

items.title: Q41 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: A new historical reading, above everything else, is influenced by the philosophy of
items.explanation: New Historicism, pioneered in Renaissance literary studies by Stephen Greenblatt in the 1980s, is profoundly shaped by Michel Foucault's theories on the circulation of power, discursive practices, and cultural surveillance.

items.title: Q42 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The Behaviourist Theory is explained in terms of
items.explanation: In psychology and language acquisition, Behaviourist Theory (developed by B.F. Skinner and Ivan Pavlov) explains all learning in terms of conditioning, where habit formation occurs through stimulus-response mechanisms and reinforcement.

items.title: Q43 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Who is the author of the poems “Elegy for Mrs. Virginia Woolf” and “William Butler in Limbo”?
items.explanation: British Second World War poet Sidney Keyes (1922–1943) wrote the elegiac poems "Elegy for Mrs. Virginia Woolf" and "William Butler in Limbo", which appeared in his posthumously acclaimed collection The Cruel Solstice (1943).

items.title: Q44 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The form of Dryden’s Essay of Dramatic Poesy is
items.explanation: John Dryden's critical treatise Of Dramatic Poesy: An Essay (1668) is written in the form of a classical Ciceronian dialogue among four gentleman critics (Crites, Eugenius, Lisideius, and Neander) floating in a barge on the River Thames.

items.title: Q45 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Which Flemish poet is Jacques Derrida related to?
items.explanation: Jacques Derrida's family genealogy and French-Algerian background link his extended family ancestry to the Flemish Belgian poet Jan Van Beers (1821–1888), a connection noted by biographers Geoffrey Bennington and Benoît Peeters.

items.title: Q46 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: In Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress which of the following are found in the Slough of Despond?
options: Hope, great expectations, and dreams of the future.
Fears and doubts, discouraging apprehensions, sinful thoughts.
items.explanation: In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Help explains that the Slough of Despond cannot be mended because all the fears, doubts, discouraging apprehensions, and sinful anxieties that accompany the conviction of sin continually settle into this mire.

items.title: Q47 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who among the following wrote a book on the life and works of Dante Gabriel Rossetti?
items.explanation: British novelist Evelyn Waugh wrote and published his first book, a critical biography titled Rossetti: His Life and Works, in 1928 to celebrate the centenary of the birth of Pre-Raphaelite poet and artist Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

items.title: Q48 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Among the Romantic poets William Blake was a total artist, undertaking many roles usually separated. In his last years he produced some of his finest engravings. Which of the following was NOT illustrated by Blake?
items.explanation: In the final years of his life, William Blake produced masterly engraved illustrations for The Book of Job (1826), Robert Thornton's edition of Virgil's Pastorals (1821), and Dante's Divine Comedy (1824–1827), but never illustrated "The rape of Leda."

items.title: Q49 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Identify the two Indian texts translated by the Orientalist William Jones I. Abhignanamshakuntalam II. Katha Sarita Sagar III. Mahabharatha IV. Manusmriti The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Sir William Jones translated Kalidasa's Sanskrit play Abhijnanasakuntalam (as Sacontalá in 1789, statement I) and the ancient Hindu code Manusmriti (as Institutes of Hindu Law in 1794, statement IV). The Katha Sarit Sagara was translated by C.H. Tawney, and the Mahabharata by K.M. Ganguli.

items.title: Q50 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which work by a famous poet does Thomas de Quincey refer to as “the feeblest and least interesting” of his writings “being substantially a mere versification, like a metrical multiplication table, of common places, the most mouldy with which criticism has baited its rat-traps”?
options: John Dryden’s An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
Alexander Pope’s An Essay on Criticism
items.explanation: In his critical essays on Alexander Pope, Thomas De Quincey condemned Pope's early poem An Essay on Criticism (1711) as "the feeblest and least interesting" of his writings, dismissing it as a mere metrical multiplication table of stale commonplaces.

items.title: Q51 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: “On or about December 1910 human character changed,” Virginia Woolf wrote. A more assertive declaration, “It was in 1915 the old world ended”, was made by a novelist in one of his/her novels, picking a date of far more historical moment, the point when an entire cultural tradition seemed to end in war. Name the novelist and the novel.
items.explanation: In Chapter 12 ("The Nightmare") of his 1923 novel Kangaroo, D.H. Lawrence wrote "It was in 1915 the old world ended", contrasting Virginia Woolf's 1910 remark by identifying the horrors of the First World War as the decisive end of European civilization.

items.title: Q52 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Semiotics, the general science of signs, traces its lineage to I. Edmund Husserl II. Charles Sanders Pierce III. Ferdinand de Saussure IV. Claude Levi-Strauss The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Modern semiotics originated in the independent work of American pragmatic philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce (semiotics, statement II) and Swiss structural linguist Ferdinand de Saussure (semiology, statement III). Husserl established phenomenology and Lévi-Strauss applied structural anthropology.

items.title: Q53 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, Norman French was the dominant language used by
items.explanation: Following the Norman Conquest of 1066, Anglo-Norman French became the exclusive language of the royal court, aristocracy, and ruling upper classes in England, while Old English remained the spoken vernacular of the common peasantry.

items.title: Q54 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which novel of George Eliot was read with pleasure by Queen Victoria and also commissioned for two paintings of scenes as a mark of recognition?
items.explanation: George Eliot's debut novel Adam Bede (1859) was enthusiastically admired by Queen Victoria, who praised it warmly in her journal and commissioned the royal artist Edward Henry Corbould to paint two watercolour scenes from the book.

items.title: Q55 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: In More’s Utopia there are 54 cities, all built on a similar plan and distributed over the island such that each city is surrounded by agricultural lands. Who does the agricultural labour in Utopia?
options: Agricultural labour is performed by slaves.
Adulterers and other criminals are forced to work on farms.
All citizens take two-year stints at farm work.
Farm labourers are brought in from allied countries.
items.explanation: In Book II of Thomas More's Utopia (1516), farming is an obligation shared equally by all citizens: every Utopian is instructed in agricultural work during youth and serves a mandatory two-year stint living and working on rural farms.

items.title: Q56 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Direct Method in English Language Teaching is also known as
items.explanation: In English language teaching, the Direct Method is commonly known as the Natural Method because it imitates first-language acquisition, immersing students directly in the target language through oral interaction and demonstration without translating into the mother tongue.

items.title: Q57 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: Vikram Seth’s From Heaven Lake is a/an
items.explanation: Vikram Seth's From Heaven Lake: Travels Through Sinkiang and Tibet (1983) is an acclaimed autobiographical travel book recounting his overland hitchhiking journey from Nanjing University across western China, Tibet, and Nepal into India.

items.title: Q58 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a punishment given by God to Adam and Eve as a consequence of tasting the forbidden fruit?
options: ‘Cursed is the ground for thy sake, thou in sorrow / Shalt eat thereof all the days of thy life’
‘Dust shalt eat all the days of life’
items.explanation: In the Book of Genesis (3:14) and Book X of John Milton's Paradise Lost, the curse "Dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life" is delivered directly to the serpent (Satan), whereas Eve is cursed with pain in childbirth and Adam with sorrowful labor before their expulsion from Eden.

items.title: Q59 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: …………… attempted to draw a distinction between two kinds of Truth, a theological Truth ‘drawn from the word and oracles of God’ and determined by faith, and a ‘scientific’ Truth based on the light of nature and the dictates of reason.
options: Treatise on the laws of Ecclesiastical Piety
Literature and Pulpit in Medieval England
items.explanation: In Book II of The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon drew a fundamental distinction between theological truth drawn from divine revelation and accepted on faith, and scientific truth derived through empirical observation of nature and human reason.

items.title: Q60 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: In Defence of Poesy what arguments does Sidney make for considering the Biblical Psalms poetry? I. They are written in meter. II. They originated in Church choirs III. They were written by a single author. IV. David uses imagery and personification to portray faith. The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In An Apology for Poetry (Defence of Poesy, c. 1579), Sir Philip Sidney argues that the Biblical Psalms are divine poetry because they are composed in meter (statement I) and use rich poetic imagery and personification to make religious faith palpable to readers (statement IV).

items.title: Q61 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: In Herman Melville’s well-known story “Bartleby the Scrivener”, what does the word “scrivener” mean?
options: Pasting clerks in a Dead Letter Office
Articled clerks in an accountant’s office
Clerks who copy legal documents by hand.
Clerks who serve as personal assistants to judges.
items.explanation: In Herman Melville's 1853 story "Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street", a scrivener was a professional legal clerk employed to hand-copy legal documents, contracts, and court records before the development of commercial typewriters.

items.title: Q62 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: “Medicine is my lawful wife” ………….. once said “and literature is my mistress.”
items.explanation: Russian dramatist and physician Anton Chekhov famously wrote in an 1888 letter to his publisher Alexei Suvorin: "Medicine is my lawful wife and literature is my mistress."

items.title: Q63 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The critical concept of a “Willing suspension of disbelief” owes its origin to Chapter …………… of Biographia Literaria.
items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge introduced the famous critical phrase "that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith" in Chapter XIV of Biographia Literaria (1817) when discussing his supernatural contributions to the Lyrical Ballads.

items.title: Q64 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Thomas Carlyle coined two evocative phrases, ‘Everlasting Nay’ and ‘Everlasting Yea’ to suggest the swing in the national mood of his times. The phrases came from
options: On Heroes, Hero-Worship and the Heroic in History
items.explanation: Thomas Carlyle coined the contrasting phrases "The Everlasting Nay" and "The Everlasting Yea" in his satirical philosophical novel Sartor Resartus (1836), charting Professor Teufelsdröckh's progression from existential doubt to spiritual reaffirmation.

items.title: Q65 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem: Marxist literary criticism stresses that I. class is an imaginary concept II. the economy is the final determinant of cultural production III. texts reveal the economic conditions of the time in which they were written. IV. the critic should see the work as self-sufficient The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Marxist literary criticism is grounded in historical materialism, arguing that economic conditions determine cultural forms (statement II) and that literary texts reflect the socioeconomic class realities of their period (statement III). Statements I and IV conflict with Marxist principles.

items.title: Q66 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: St. Augustine brought Christianity, and the Latin language enriched Old English by giving it the capacity to talk about ……………
items.explanation: When St. Augustine brought Christian missionaries to Anglo-Saxon England in 597 AD, the widespread introduction of Latin equipped Old English with a rich vocabulary for articulating complex theological, philosophical, and abstract ideas.

items.title: Q67 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who makes the following speech in Henrik Ibsen’s Ghosts? “I almost think we are all ghosts, all of us … It isn’t just what we have inherited from our father and mother that walks in us. It’s all sorts of dead ideas, and all sorts of old and obsolete beliefs. They’re not alive in us; but they are lodged in us and we can never free ourselves from them …. There must be ghosts the whole country over, as thick as the sands of the sea.”
items.explanation: In Act II of Henrik Ibsen's naturalistic play Ghosts (1881), Mrs. Helene Alving speaks this monologue to Pastor Manders, explaining that society is haunted by obsolete traditions, dead customs, and hypocritical Victorian moral beliefs that inhabit our minds like ghosts.

items.title: Q68 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which of these lines is NOT in Pope’s Essay on Criticism?
options: “Wretches hang that jury men may dine”
“A little learning is a dangerous thing”
“Fools rush in where angels fear to tread”
“The sound must seem an echo to the sense”
items.explanation: The satirical couplet "And wretches hang that jury-men may dine" appears in Canto III (line 22) of Alexander Pope's mock-epic The Rape of the Lock (1714), whereas the other three famous maxims are from An Essay on Criticism (1711).

items.title: Q69 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: One of the principles of materials preparation for language learning is that
options: any kind of material can be chosen
grading of materials should be done
a small amount of material should be introduced
items.explanation: A foundational principle in ELT materials preparation and syllabus design is the systematic grading of language items, ensuring that learning materials progress from simple to complex according to the learners' communicative needs and proficiency.

items.title: Q70 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: R.K. Narayan’s “A Horse and Two Goats” is set in a tiny village called …………..
items.explanation: R.K. Narayan's short story "A Horse and Two Goats" (1970), which dramatizes the comic miscommunication between the old villager Muni and a wealthy American tourist, is set in the tiny south Indian village of Kritam.

items.title: Q71 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Kishori Mohan Ganguli, an Indian translator working in the last quarter of 19 century, is best known for his free English translation of
items.explanation: Kishori Mohan Ganguli was an Indian translator who produced the first complete, unabridged English prose translation of the Sanskrit epic the Mahabharata, published in eighteen volumes between 1883 and 1896 by Pratap Chandra Roy.

items.title: Q72 · August 2016 (Paper III - Re-Exam)
items.meta: Reading Comprehension · Reading Comprehension
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Poem]
Read the following poem carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Remembered Village" by R. Parthasarathy

If you love your country, he said, why are you here?
Say, you are tired of hearing about
all that wonder-that-was-India crap.
It is tea that's gone cold: time to brew a fresh pot.
But what wouldn't you give for one or two places in it?
Aunt's house near Kulittalai, for instance.
It often gets its feet wet in the river,
and coils of rain hiss and slither on the roof.
Even the well boils over.
Her twelve-house lane is bloated with the full moon,
and bamboos tie up the eerie riverfront
with a knot of toads.
A Black Pillaiyar temple squats at one end of the village —
stone drum that is beaten thin on festivals by the devout.
Bells curl their lips at the priest's rustic Sanskrit.
Outside, pariah dogs kick up an incense of howls.
And beyond the paddy fields,
dead on time, the Erode Mail rumbles past,
a light needle of smoke threading remote villages
such as yours that are routinely dropped by schedules,
and no trains are ever missed.

Question:
The opening question best suggests
items.explanation: In the opening line of R. Parthasarathy's poem "Remembered Village" ("If you love your country, he said, why are you here?"), the question directly introduces the speaker's emotional conflict and physical state of exile living away from India.

Read the following poem carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Remembered Village" by R. Parthasarathy

If you love your country, he said, why are you here?
Say, you are tired of hearing about
all that wonder-that-was-India crap.

Aunt's house near Kulittalai, for instance.
It often gets its feet wet in the river,
and coils of rain hiss and slither on the roof.
Even the well boils over.
Her twelve-house lane is bloated with the full moon,
and bamboos tie up the eerie riverfront
with a knot of toads.
A Black Pillaiyar temple squats at one end of the village —
stone drum that is beaten thin on festivals by the devout.
Bells curl their lips at the priest's rustic Sanskrit.

And beyond the paddy fields,

Question:
The words “no trains are ever missed” in their context mean that
options: the poet is punctual about boarding trains
all trains stop in the village but none is missed
the remote village is not a stop for trains; so no train is ever missed
the poet remembers all the trains boarded from the village
items.explanation: In the closing stanza of "Remembered Village", the phrase "no trains are ever missed" carries bitter irony: the Erode Mail rumbles past without stopping because remote villages like Kulittalai are omitted from the rail schedule entirely, so a train cannot be missed where it never stops.
